I. Salzberger-Wittenberg: Psycho-Analytic Insight and Relationships: A Kleinian Approach. Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1970. Price £1.50.

Betty Joseph

Betty Joseph

Betty Joseph  

There is always a problem in carrying knowledge acquired in one field over to an allied field in such a way as to be sound, comprehensible and really useful. This book courageously and, I think, successfully aims to do this. The idea of “Psycho-Analytic Insight and Relationships”, which is one of the series of the Library of Social Work, is to indicate some of the ways in which psychoanalytic theory as developed by Melanie Klein can help social workers to understand their clients and their relationships with them. The author herself was a caseworker before going on to train in child psycho-therapy, so that her book has the advantage of being written by someone who has worked in depth with children, as well as knowing at first hand the extraordinarily rich and complex problem of trying to help people who present with difficulties in their lives as well as in their environments. In this field the aims of the worker have to be rethought with each new case.

Mrs. Wittenberg describes in her introduction the background to this work; she brought together a small group of experienced caseworkers from different fields and had joint discussions with them. The problems and examples arising from these discussions, illuminated by the author's psycho-analytic insight, form the basis of this book. This method of working gives considerable richness to the book, since the theory which the author outlines is always based on, or linked with, human material and therefore generally gives a feeling of immediate relevance to casework. This one senses as soon as one gets into the book—the first two sections of Part I deal with feelings—the feelings that the caseworker brings into the relationship with the client, and the client into the relationship with the caseworker. These are illustrated and briefly discussed, and the whole of the first part of the book deals with “Aspects of a Relationship”. Here, as throughout, a major unspoken point emerges—the importance of the link between analytic knowledge and spontaneous human understanding and insight. The book is in itself a demonstration of how the caseworker's ability to tolerate and help with pain and discomfort, as well as hope and progress, in her clients, must be based on real humanity, but that humanity and warmth is not enough.

Delys Daws

Delys Daws

Delys Daws  

This book is initially a report of the transactions of the Topeka Conference on Cultural Factors in Delinquency, and thus represents the sum of the ideas of people from varying disciplines. However it has been written up skilfully

67

by the two editors, T. C. N. Gibbens and Robert H. Ahrenfeldt, so that the first half in particular has a continuous and individual flavour.

Perhaps the most interesting part of the book to those working in the psychological field is the chapter on Internal and External Controls. It is emphasised that there are “individual and cultural aspects of both kinds of control” and that these “do not correspond to a simple dichotomy of the psychological and the sociocultural approach”. The authors feel that consistency and persistence are needed if controls are to be adequately internalised and that the quality of internal controls also depends upon consistency in parental emotional attitudes, by which the child builds up an understanding of the moods, feelings and motives of others. The ways in which the culture may go on to reinforce or undermine controls is then shown. Without going into depth this book does show in an interesting way some of the connection between the individual's own progress towards integration and the cultural framework within which this takes place.

“Non-communicating Children” describes research based on the investigation of 474 children at the Children's Units at Belmont Hospital, Sutton, Surrey, during the years 1953-1967. The authors are both psychiatrists and the work was initiated by Dr. Minski in his capacity as consultant psychiatrist to the Royal National Throat, Nose and Ear Hospital when he was often asked for a differential diagnosis between, for example, subnormality and deafness in young children. The Units were set up on a research grant and later became part of the National Health Service. Various types of children with communication difficulties were referred for longer and more thorough diagnosis than is usually possible elsewhere. Twelve beds are available for in-patients, as the authors state it is sometimes necessary to keep the children for months or even years.

The book includes chapters by Dr. Agatha H. Bowley, Ph.D., on “The Psychological Assessment of Young Autistic Children”, by Joan E. Taylor, B.A., teacher-in-charge at the Units, on “Auditory Assessment” and on classroom work, and a chapter on research by Dr. Ian Evans, Ph.D.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Place of Once-Weekly Treatment in the Work of an Analytically Trained Child Psychotherapist**

Martha Harris

Martha Harris

Martha Harris  

This brief paper reintroduces a topic which was the focus of the Association's very first study weekend eleven years ago, one with which those of us who work in clinics are continually occupied, and about which after those years of experience we may be in a better position to ask the relevant questions, and to make a few tentative generalisations.

I would first of all like to consider some of the anxieties that it tends to arouse in the therapist whose own personal analysis was a more intensive experience and who received a training largely based on cases who were receiving the same kind of intensive treatment. I would then like to consider some of the real differences and difficulties attendant upon the less intensive arrangement of sessions; possible goals; methods of selecting cases; the value and the dangers of teamwork. I would then like to mention situations where modification of the analytic technique of interpretation within the transference may seem to be more appropriate. Finally, I would like to take a glance at the relevance of our training for this once-weekly work, and at the place which it may usefully occupy within the timetable of the individual therapist.

Anxieties Aroused in the Therapist by Once-Weekly Treatment

There is often the guilty feeling that we should be giving this child more for his need is great. Perhaps we are still in full analysis ourselves; at any rate we have had in the past a more leisurely opportunity to come to grips with our own problems in living. We may be treating other children on a more intensive basis and feel: why should those have an opportunity that is denied to this one? And here we need to take cognisance of our own still operative Oedipal and sibling rivalries. An obsessive need for equality and fairness which does not take practicality into account is often a sign that these are interfering with our judgment.

To make up for “selling him short” we may try too hard to get results, to become over-active, to reassure ourselves that we are doing something for him. This may take the form of cramming in too many theoretical interpretations, of becoming impatient with what we are able to do in the session and trying to operate through the social worker and the parents. It may take the form of bringing into the child's session information gained through the social worker and the parents, information which the child has not given us but which we feel he ought to be dealing with.

Some Comments on the State of Clinical Casework Today**

Sara Rosenfeld

Sara Rosenfeld

Sara Rosenfeld  

Introduction

The coming of age of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (Non-Medical) is an apppropriate occasion to pause and evaluate some aspects of clinical casework as it is conducted by a group of child psychotherapists within the Association. Since there are very great variations in the theory and technique as practised by our members, it seems to be most fruitful to confine this survey to my colleagues and my own experience at the Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic. Thus there will be emphasis on one clinical and theoretical viewpoint. It has to be remembered however that, as Freud stated, there is no monopoly any one of us possesses in the field of psychotherapy. He reminds us, “There are many ways and means of practising psychotherapy. All that lead to recovery are good … Because of the part I have played in founding this (psychoanalytic) therapy, I feel a personal obligation to devote myself to closer investigation of it and to the development of its technique”. (Freud, S., 1905.)

At the time we entered the field of psychoanalysis, certain shifts in emphasis had already taken place. Psychoanalysts were not so much concerned with infantile psychopathology as such, but rather with the need to regard child analysis as a source of information and confirmation of theories for the understanding and treatment of adult neurotics. The existence of infantile sexuality was accepted and indeed it was already beginning to influence methods of child rearing of our generation. The contribution of infantile sexuality to the establishment of an infantile neurosis which proved to be universally present in neurotic adult patients was also established fact.

A further shift from the focus of interest on content of the Id to the dynamics and operation of the ego had already taken place and was crystallised in Anna Freud's book The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence. It established beyond doubt that childhood neurosis existed in its own right and showed a similar development to adult neurosis. That is, briefly, in the child as in the adult conflict was followed by regression to earlier fixation points—the regressive aims aroused anxiety which was warded off by defences and resulted in a compromise solution in the form of symptom formation. Anna Freud defined the task of psychoanalysis as follows, “To acquire the fullest possible knowledge of all three institutions of which we believe the psychic personality to be constituted and to learn what are their relations to one another and to the outside world.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with A Seven-and-a-half-year-old Girl in the Care of a Local Authority Children's Department

Rachel Newbolt

Rachel Newbolt

Rachel Newbolt  

Introduction

The case of Sandra who came in to the Care of a local authority at the age of three and a half, affords some interesting similarities and contrasts with the case described by Patricia Rad ford (1969). It also raises questions concerning society's treatment of parents found to be neglectful. The first person to seek the help of the clinic was the probation officer who was supervising Sandra's mother, Mrs. M., after a charge of wilful neglect. The parents had failed to seek help when Sandra's refusal to eat had reduced her weight to twenty-two pounds. There had been signs of active physical ill-treatment in addition.

History

The probable reasons for this unhappy state of affairs appear in the early history. An outline of events until Sandra came in to treatment four years later will also be given. Sandra was a second born, dizygotic twin, who had a difficult breech birth and had to be placed in an incubator for the first four days of life. When Mrs. M. and the twins returned home, the paternal grandmother took over the entire care of Sandra. It was apparently typical of Mrs. M. that she allowed this situation to continue for years without a cross word, although inwardly feeling most resentful. Some time during Sandra's third year, grandmother moved away from the family to a home of her own. The family now consisted of five children, the eldest a boy, born two and a half years before the twins, then a girl, Beatrice, born eleven months after them, and finally a boy, Terry, born sixteen months after that. The family was then living in a high flat where they had been rehoused after acute housing difficulties had caused the parents to live apart during Mrs. M.'s pregnancy with the twins.

When Sandra was three, her grandmother made a report to the N.S.P.C.C. without informing her parents. Shortly afterwards, Sandra was admitted to hospital, suffering from a variety of bruises, burns and abrasions, such as we now associate with the “Battered Baby Syndrome”. She weighed only twenty-two pounds. Tests ruled out physical disease. She ate so voraciously that the paediatrician thought that she had been systematically starved. It turned out later that she had been refusing to eat at all in her own home but had gone round begging food from neighbours. The parents were prosecuted and a supervision order was made for one year, each parent being assigned to a probation officer. A few months after this, the family were given a transfer to a council house with a garden.

[[RunningHead]]

Comments on the History of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (Non-Medical)**

Jess Guthrie

Jess Guthrie

Jess Guthrie  

At this anniversary meeting, it may be of interest to our guests as well as to some of our younger members to have a brief account of the history of the Association. As this morning's programme allows for only ten minutes, it will be brief indeed and much, including the names of many people who have helped us in our development, will have to be left out.

Thinking around our beginnings takes us back to the early nineteen-thirties. At that time efforts were already being made towards the establishment of a professional body which would be concerned with the standards of work and conduct of those undertaking psychotherapeutic treatment with children. A small number of people had been qualified at the Institute of Child Psychology where the only existing course of training had been set up by Dr. Margaret Lowenfeld. Others had to get what training they could under their own initiative and with the help and supervision of the psychiatrists with whom they worked. The outbreak of war postponed any moves towards the setting up of a professional association. Psychotherapists, together with psychologists, teachers and social workers, were plunged into attempts to help in the problems raised by the evacuation of thousands of children into isolation from their families and from much that was familiar in their lives. Thirty years later, it is hard to remember that a great deal that is now accepted as basic knowledge has been formulated and published since that time. With grossly inadequate training and knowledge it was necessary to do what one could in meeting the needs of ordinary children suddenly separated from their parents, and of some children too disturbed to settle in strange families, as well as in giving support to the adults involved in their daily care.

Largely out of the experience of the war nurseries run by Anna Freud and Dorothy Burlingham, the Hampstead Child Therapy Course was established in 1947 and two years later the course at the Tavistock Clinic was instituted. During these years following the end of the war an increasing number of child guidance clinics were set up throughout the country, and psychologists and psychiatric social workers were being asked to undertake the treatment of children. The need for a professional body concerned with standards of work and training was then even more urgent than it had been in the nineteen-thirties. In response to this need a sub-committee of the Committee of Professional Psychologists, under the chairmanship of John Gibbs, met to consider the matter.

[[RunningHead]]

Once-Weekly Work with A Rebellious Adolescent Girl**

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin  

Jane was referred to the Child Guidance Clinic when she was 13 1/2 by the family doctor, at the request of her parents, who were finding themselves unable to control her, and were very anxious about her future at school. Jane was at a grammar school and the headmistress had threatened to expel her. In a letter, Mother described Jane as “very difficult and unable to take discipline”. She was lying continually. She had threatened Mother with the carving knife three times. She was said to hate “parents, home, school, her brother and even Edgware”. She had a group of friends who were not acceptable to her parents. Mother wrote, “she particularly admires boys with motor-bikes, leather jackets and long greasy hair”.

Jane and her parents were invited to a diagnostic interview by the psychiatrist. Mother and Jane appeared. Jane was uncommunicative and angry. She felt that Mother understood her although she said she didn't, but Father did not understand at all. Mother talked to the P.S.W. at length. She felt Jane was very unhappy. She was making no progress at school, and at home there were constant battles over school regulations. Jane had given up the things she used to enjoy—play-writing, horse-riding and swimming—and now spent all her time with a gang hanging around cafes. Mother and Jane quarrelled over clothes, make-up and smoking. Mother thought everything had got worse when Father was abroad six months ago; it was then that Jane started doing just what she wanted. Jane was said to hate Father; Father used to think the world of her, but had now given her up and thought she would go to the bad.

Mother gave some details of Jane's early history. She was breast-fed for three months: “It was sick and screaming all the time”. Bottle-feeding gave little relief until she was ten months. “She was restless all day and I had to be with her all the time”. She was a very active baby and settled much better when she was mobile. When Jane was nearly four, Mother had another baby. The pregnancy was complicated and Mother had some time in hospital. Father looked after Jane.

[[RunningHead]]

Extending Fields of Work**

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg  

The task I have been set is to give some indication of the variety of settings and the different kinds of work in which our members are engaged and the directions in which we seem to be developing. I would like briefly to survey the field of our activities and then bring illustrations from my own experience to show in which way I see these extensions linked to our primary aim and experience, namely, psychotherapy of children and adolescents.

Survey of Areas of Work

Firstly, we have extended the range of ages we study and deal with. We have a particular interest in infants and very young children. Weekly observations of mothers and babies in their own home for one to two years (first introduced by Dr. E. Bick) form an essential part of our training at the Tavistock and the Hampstead Clinic. Discussions in seminars of these detailed observations of the interaction between mother and baby have proved of immense value to all those who have undertaken it. It has been a revelation to most to discover how much the baby contributes to the relationship and that it is possible to study the adjustments and mal-adjustments as they develop. It has also been a very good way of preparing students for their clinical observations, increasing their awareness of non-verbal communications and making them receptive to recognising the infantile aspects of their patients’ personalities.

At the other end of the age range, there has been a great expansion of work with adolescents. Their problems and those they present for their parents, teachers and society has resulted in adolescent psychiatry becoming a new specialisation. But where does adolescence end? More and more we find ourselves drawn into work with students and young adults (especially since the age of majority has dropped to 18 years) and the question arises whether it is appropriate to call ourselves child psychotherapists. I wonder whether the time has come to change our name and perhaps include the treatment of young adults in our training programme?

Doris Wills  

It was indeed fortunate that Dr. Winnicott was able to see this fascinating book through the press before his death. It was planned for many years, and is based on a gradual formulation and bringing together of his ideas in this important area, since Dr. Winnicott sees play as a function of child and adult alike, and as closely linked with culture.

As always Dr. Winnicott shows his ability to observe with a fresh and innocent eye, unblinkered by accepted theory which often restricts the focus of our attention. He changes that focus with enormous enlightenment to us as observers. In addition he has the poet's subtlety, and the poet's humility in leaving certain paradoxes, certain unillumined areas, and allowing them to remain on the borders of our present understanding.

Dr. Winnicott describes the book as a development of his paper “Transitional Objects and Transitional Phenomena”, saying that the area of individual development and experience seems to have been neglected by analysts, while attention was focussed on psychic reality and its relation to external, or shared, reality. He sees a continuum between transitional phenomena, playing, and later cultural experience, and feels that the latter has not found its true place in analytic theory.

Dr. Winnicott states that he wishes to reverse the sequence psychoanalysis— psychotherapy—play material—playing, saying that it is play that is universal and that facilitates growth, while psychoanalysis has been developed as a highly specialised form of playing in the service of communication. He thinks that when a patient cannot “play” this is a major symptom which must be dealt with first (play is used here to describe much of the thinking brought by both children and adults during treatment). Dr. Winnicott points out that playing is inherently exciting and precarious, and that this does not derive from instinctual arousal “but from the precariousness that belongs to the interplay in the child's mind of that which is subjective … and that which is objectively perceived”. He stresses the idea of creativity, saying that the meaning of this should not get lost through relating it only to the successful creation, it should describe the colouring of the whole attitude to external reality.
